questions.q: Which of the following viruses is naked, that is, it has no lipid envelope?
questions.x: Poliovirus consists only of an icosahedral protein capsid around its RNA. Influenza virus, HIV and herpes virus all carry an envelope taken from host membranes.

questions.q: The three basic types of capsid symmetry in viruses are:
questions.x: Capsids are helical (such as TMV), icosahedral or polyhedral (such as adenovirus), or complex (such as bacteriophage T4). Coccus, bacillus and spirillum are shapes of bacteria.

questions.q: In human skeletal muscle short of oxygen, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid in the:
questions.x: Lactic acid fermentation, like glycolysis, takes place in the cytoplasm. Without oxygen, pyruvate does not need to enter the mitochondria.

questions.q: At the end of each turn of the Krebs cycle, which compound is regenerated so that the cycle can continue?
questions.x: The four-carbon oxaloacetate is re-formed at the last step and can combine with a new acetyl CoA. That is why the pathway is a cycle.

questions.q: Which of the following compounds is inorganic even though it contains carbon?
questions.x: Carbon dioxide has no carbon–hydrogen bonds and is treated as an inorganic compound. Glucose, urea and glycerol are organic compounds containing carbon bonded to hydrogen.

questions.q: Bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) in blood plasma are important because they:
o: Act as a buffer, helping to keep the pH of blood steady
Form the main structure of bone
Act as the main energy source of red blood cells
questions.x: Bicarbonate ions take up or release H⁺ ions, which resists changes in blood pH. Oxygen is carried by haemoglobin, bone is mainly calcium phosphate, and red cells use glucose for energy.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a role of membrane glycoproteins?
o: Serving as the cell's main energy store
Acting as antigens that mark the cell
Helping cells recognise and stick to one another
questions.x: Membrane glycoproteins work as receptors, antigens and recognition and adhesion molecules. Energy is stored as glycogen, starch or fat, not as membrane glycoproteins.

questions.q: The enzyme that makes RNA by copying a DNA template is:
questions.x: RNA polymerase joins ribonucleotides complementary to the DNA template during transcription. Reverse transcriptase does the opposite, making DNA from RNA.

questions.q: The spikes on the envelope of influenza virus, which attach the virus to host cells, are made of:
questions.x: The envelope spikes of influenza and many other viruses are glycoproteins that bind to receptors on the host cell. The envelope itself is mainly phospholipid.

questions.q: Palmitic acid (C15H31COOH), common in animal fat, is classed as a:
questions.x: Palmitic acid fits the saturated formula CnH2n+1COOH (n = 15, 2n+1 = 31), so its chain has no C=C double bonds. Its –COOH group makes it an acid, not an alcohol.

questions.q: The layer of fat around organs such as the kidneys mainly serves to:
questions.x: Fat around delicate organs acts as a cushion or shock absorber, holding them in place and protecting them from injury.

questions.q: On complete hydrolysis, a substance yields only glucose. It could be any of the following EXCEPT:
questions.x: Starch, glycogen and maltose are made only of glucose units, so their hydrolysis gives only glucose. Sucrose gives glucose and fructose, so it cannot be the substance.

questions.q: Fats release more energy per gram than carbohydrates on oxidation mainly because fats contain:
o: More oxygen atoms per carbon atom
Nitrogen atoms that release extra energy
Many more C–H bonds and relatively little oxygen
questions.x: Fatty acid chains are rich in C–H bonds and poor in oxygen, so they are less oxidised to begin with and release more energy when fully oxidised. Carbohydrates already contain much oxygen.

questions.q: Liver glycogen and muscle glycogen differ in their main role because:
o: Liver glycogen is broken down to keep blood glucose steady, while muscle glycogen is used mainly by the muscle itself
Muscle glycogen is released into the blood, while liver glycogen is never broken down
Liver glycogen is a structural material, while muscle glycogen is a hormone
Muscle glycogen is converted into cellulose, while liver glycogen is converted into protein
questions.x: Between meals the liver breaks down its glycogen and releases glucose into the blood. Muscle glycogen supplies glucose for the muscle's own contraction.

questions.q: A C=C double bond in the chain of a natural unsaturated fatty acid usually:
o: Makes the chain straight, so the molecules pack tightly
Makes the chain soluble in water
Adds a second carboxyl group to the chain
Puts a bend in the chain, so the molecules cannot pack closely
questions.x: The double bond introduces a kink in the hydrocarbon chain. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly, which is why unsaturated fats have lower melting points.

questions.q: In a ribosome, ribosomal RNA is found in:
o: Both the large and the small subunits
questions.x: Each ribosome has a large and a small subunit, and both are made of rRNA combined with proteins. Ribosomes have no membrane.

questions.q: Flight muscle cells of insects need much ATP. Compared with less active cells, their mitochondria would be expected to have:
questions.x: More cristae mean more inner membrane area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so active cells have mitochondria with many cristae.

questions.q: Secretory vesicles bud off from the Golgi apparatus at its:
questions.x: Vesicles from the ER join the cis face; the finished products leave in vesicles from the trans face, which faces the plasma membrane.

questions.q: Bacteria can be classified by shape. A rod-shaped bacterium is called a:
questions.x: Rod-shaped bacteria are bacilli, spherical ones are cocci, spiral ones are spirilla, and comma-shaped ones are vibrios.

questions.q: Proteins loosely attached to the inner or outer surface of the plasma membrane, without passing through the lipid bilayer, are called:
questions.x: Peripheral proteins sit on the surface and are easily removed. Integral proteins, including channel proteins, are embedded in or span the bilayer.

questions.q: A microphone changes sound energy into electrical signals. A sensory receptor is compared to a microphone because both:
o: Amplify signals without changing their form
Change one form of energy into another
questions.x: Both are transducers: they convert one form of energy into another. A receptor changes the energy of a stimulus into the electrical energy of nerve impulses.

questions.q: A photoreceptor is a receptor that is sensitive to:
questions.x: Photoreceptors, such as the rods and cones of the retina, respond to light. Sound is detected by mechanoreceptors and dissolved chemicals by chemoreceptors.

questions.q: Coughing, sneezing and blinking are grouped together because all three are:
o: Cranial reflexes with their centres in the brain
Spinal reflexes with their centres in the spinal cord
questions.x: All three are inborn reflexes integrated in the brainstem and using cranial nerves, so they are cranial reflexes. They are not learned, and they are not stretch reflexes.

questions.q: The sensory neuron of a reflex arc is also called the:
questions.x: The sensory neuron carries impulses towards the CNS, so it is afferent. The motor neuron is efferent, and the relay neuron is the interneuron inside the CNS.

questions.q: Before any training began, the bell in Pavlov's experiment was:
o: An unconditioned stimulus that caused salivation
A conditioned stimulus that caused salivation
A reflex centre in the dog's brain
A neutral stimulus that caused no salivation
questions.x: At first the bell had nothing to do with feeding and produced no salivation, so it was neutral. Only after repeated pairing with food did it become a conditioned stimulus.

questions.q: The brief hyperpolarisation at the end of an action potential occurs because:
o: K+ channels close slowly, so slightly too much K+ leaves
Na+ channels open a second time
Ca2+ ions flood into the axon
questions.x: The voltage-gated K+ channels stay open a little after the resting value is reached, so extra K+ leaves and the inside becomes briefly more negative.

questions.q: Blinking, coughing and the pupil reflex belong to one group of reflexes. What is true of this group?
o: They are all learned through experience after birth
Their centres lie in the brain and their pathways use cranial nerves
They are integrated in the grey matter of the spinal cord
questions.x: These are cranial reflexes: they are integrated in the brain and use cranial nerves. They are inborn, not learned, and many have interneurons, so they are not always monosynaptic.

questions.q: Damage to the hypothalamus stops the production of antidiuretic hormone. Which effect is most likely?
o: Large volumes of dilute urine and strong thirst
Small volumes of very concentrated urine
Inability to see in bright light
questions.x: Antidiuretic hormone from the hypothalamus makes the kidneys reabsorb water. Without it, much water is lost as dilute urine and the person becomes very thirsty. Balance and vision depend on other brain parts.

questions.q: Buffer solutions are used in enzyme experiments in order to:
questions.x: A buffer resists pH changes, so pH does not vary during the experiment and does not affect the results.

questions.q: The optimum pH of most enzymes that work inside human cells is close to:
questions.x: The cytoplasm is close to neutral, and most intracellular enzymes work best near pH 7. Pepsin, with an optimum near 2, is an exception suited to the stomach.

questions.q: The effect of a non-competitive inhibitor on an enzyme reaction is similar to:
o: Raising the temperature to the optimum
Reducing the amount of working enzyme
questions.x: A non-competitive inhibitor puts some enzyme molecules out of action whatever the substrate level, just as if less enzyme were present.

questions.q: A change of pH can slow an enzyme reaction even when the enzyme's shape is not changed, because:
o: The charges on the substrate may change, so it binds less well to the active site
pH changes the temperature of the mixture
pH increases the amount of substrate
pH always breaks the peptide bonds of the substrate
questions.x: Binding depends on matching charges on both the enzyme and the substrate. If pH changes the substrate's ionisation, binding and reaction rate fall.

questions.q: Between about 0 °C and 40 °C, the rate of many enzyme-controlled reactions roughly:
o: Halves for every 10 °C rise in temperature
Doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature
questions.x: Below the optimum, a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate (a temperature coefficient of about 2), because molecules move faster and collide more often.

questions.q: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old and the oldest fossil cells are about 3.5 billion years old. Roughly how long after the Earth formed did cells appear?
questions.x: 4.6 − 3.5 = 1.1 billion years. The figure 3.5 billion years is the age of the fossils, not the gap before life began.

questions.q: Before Lamarck, most naturalists in Europe believed that species were:
o: Fixed and unchanging since they were created
questions.x: The common view was the fixity of species, each kind created separately. Lamarck was among the first to argue clearly that species change.

questions.q: Weismann used the term germplasm for:
o: The cytoplasm of the body cells
The material that makes up the skin and muscles
The hereditary material in germ cells that passes from generation to generation
The food stored in an egg
questions.x: Weismann said the germplasm, carried in the germ cells, is continuous from one generation to the next and gives rise to both the gametes and the body. Changes in the body cells (somatoplasm) die with the individual.

questions.q: Throughout pregnancy, progesterone helps to:
o: Cause the endometrium to be shed
Keep the uterine muscle relaxed so the embryo is not expelled
questions.x: Progesterone maintains the endometrium and reduces contractions of the myometrium. A fall in its level is one factor in starting menstruation or labour.

questions.q: Four days after sexual exposure, a man has painful urination with a thick yellow discharge. Pus from the urethra shows Gram-negative diplococci. The disease is:
questions.x: Gram-negative diplococci in urethral pus with painful discharge soon after exposure point to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Syphilis is caused by a spiral bacterium and herpes by a virus.

questions.q: Normal spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules needs:
questions.x: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and testosterone from the Leydig cells acts within the tubules; both are required for full sperm production.

questions.q: Near ovulation, the cervical mucus becomes thin and watery, making it easier for sperm to pass. This change is caused by:
questions.x: Rising oestrogen before ovulation makes cervical mucus thin and stretchy. After ovulation, progesterone makes it thick again.

questions.q: Which bone does NOT take part in forming the knee joint?
questions.x: The knee joint is formed by the femur, the tibia and the patella (kneecap). The fibula lies alongside the tibia but does not reach the knee joint itself.

questions.q: In the word 'arthritis', the ending '-itis' means:
questions.x: 'Arthr-' means joint and '-itis' means inflammation, so arthritis is inflammation of a joint. The same ending is used in words such as tonsillitis and hepatitis.

questions.q: In a relaxed sarcomere, each thin filament runs from:
o: The M line to the Z line on the same side
A Z line partway into the A band
One Z line to the next Z line
The H zone to the M line
questions.x: Thin filaments are anchored at the Z line and extend through the I band into the outer part of the A band, overlapping the thick filaments. In a relaxed sarcomere they do not reach the H zone or the M line.

questions.q: Which group contains ONLY bones of the appendicular skeleton?
o: Clavicle, femur, carpals and hip bones
questions.x: The appendicular skeleton is the limbs plus the pectoral and pelvic girdles. The sternum, ribs and hyoid are all axial, so each wrong group contains one axial bone.

questions.q: Skeletal muscles that move a bone usually work in antagonistic pairs because a muscle:
o: Can contract only once and then must be replaced
Can only pull when it contracts and cannot push
Pushes the bone when it relaxes
Needs a second muscle to supply its ATP
questions.x: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls; it cannot actively push. So a second muscle on the other side of the joint is needed to pull the bone back.

questions.q: A sarcomere is 2.4 µm long and its H zone is 0.4 µm wide. Assuming the thin filaments from both Z lines are equal, how long is each thin filament?
questions.x: The two thin filaments together cover the sarcomere except the H zone: 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 µm, so each is 1.0 µm. The value 2.0 µm forgets to divide between the two sides.

questions.q: Which form of arthritis results from a metabolic disorder, rather than from wear or from an immune attack?
questions.x: Gout comes from a disorder of uric acid metabolism, leading to high blood uric acid. Osteoarthritis is degenerative wear, and rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune.

questions.q: The A band and I band of a sarcomere are named after how they affect polarised light. The letters stand for:
questions.x: The dark A band is anisotropic (it bends polarised light) and the light I band is isotropic. The names have nothing to do with actin or with activity.

questions.q: What is the probability that a gamete from an AaBbCc individual, with independent genes, carries A, B and C together?
questions.x: Each gene puts its dominant allele into a gamete with probability 1/2, independently, so the chance is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

questions.q: The recombination frequency is 8% between genes P and Q, and 3% between Q and R. The recombination frequency between P and R could be:
questions.x: If R lies between P and Q, P–R is 8 − 3 = 5%. If Q lies between P and R, P–R is 8 + 3 = 11%. A third distance is needed to decide.

questions.q: During crossing over, the broken segments of non-sister chromatids are joined again by the enzyme:
questions.x: In crossing over the chromatids break (by endonuclease) and the exchanged pieces are sealed by DNA ligase. Helicase unwinds DNA and polymerases build new strands.

questions.q: The daughter of a hemophilic man clots normally, and her husband is normal. Before birth, when the sex is unknown, the chance that their baby is hemophilic is:
questions.x: She received Xʰ from her father, so she is a carrier. A child has a 1/2 chance of being a son and a 1/2 chance of getting Xʰ: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.q: Two genes lie on the same chromosome, yet a dihybrid test cross gives a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. The best explanation is that:
o: Crossing over does not occur on that chromosome
They are so far apart that a crossover between them occurs in nearly every meiosis
questions.x: Very distant genes on one chromosome recombine about 50% of the time, so they give the same ratio as unlinked genes.

questions.q: Mendel removed the anthers from the flowers of one parent plant before they matured. The purpose was to:
o: Increase the number of seeds produced
Prevent self-pollination so that the cross could be controlled
questions.x: Pea flowers normally self-pollinate. Removing the immature anthers (emasculation) stopped this, so Mendel could dust pollen from the chosen male parent and control the cross.

questions.q: In a dihybrid whose two linked genes are in the repulsion (trans) arrangement, the homologous chromosomes carry:
o: AB on one homologue and ab on the other
One dominant and one recessive allele each (Ab and aB)
The two genes on two different chromosome pairs
questions.x: In repulsion each homologue has one dominant and one recessive allele (Ab/aB). AB on one homologue and ab on the other is the coupling (cis) arrangement.

questions.q: When the heart rate rises during exercise, the length of each cardiac cycle falls. This shortening comes mainly from a shorter:
questions.x: As the heart speeds up, systole shortens only a little; most of the time saved comes from a shorter diastole (the resting and filling phase).

questions.q: Which valves are open while the atria are contracting?
questions.x: In atrial systole the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves are open so blood enters the ventricles. The semilunar valves stay closed because the ventricles are relaxed.

questions.q: In a healthy adult heart, which two chambers contain oxygenated blood?
questions.x: Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium and passes to the left ventricle. The whole right side carries deoxygenated blood from the body.

questions.q: The AV node is situated in the:
o: Wall of the left ventricle near the apex
Lower part of the right atrium, near the interatrial septum
Upper wall of the left atrium
questions.x: The AV node lies in the floor of the right atrium close to the interatrial septum, at the junction of atria and ventricles. The SA node is higher up in the right atrial wall.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle cells of the heart wall are joined end to end by:
o: Tendons, which attach them to the ribs
Chordae tendineae, which hold them in place
Intercalated discs, which let impulses pass quickly from cell to cell
questions.x: Intercalated discs join neighbouring cardiac muscle cells and let the impulse spread rapidly, so the muscle contracts as one unit. Chordae tendineae belong to the valves.

questions.q: The chemical messengers released by helper T cells to activate other lymphocytes are called:
questions.x: Helper T cells release cytokines, such as interleukins, that stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Antibodies come from plasma cells and histamine from mast cells.

questions.q: Plasma cells develop from:
questions.x: When a B cell meets its antigen it divides, and many of its offspring become antibody-secreting plasma cells. T cells do not form plasma cells.

questions.q: In active body tissues, carbon dioxide moves from the cells into the capillary blood because:
o: Red blood cells pump it in by active transport
Its partial pressure in the blood is higher than in the cells
Its partial pressure in the cells is higher than in the blood
Haemoglobin attracts it more strongly than oxygen
questions.x: Respiring cells produce CO₂, so their pCO₂ (about 46 mm Hg or more) is higher than that of arriving arterial blood (about 40 mm Hg). CO₂ therefore diffuses into the blood.

questions.q: The fact that haemoglobin releases more oxygen when the carbon dioxide concentration of the blood rises is called the:
questions.x: The Bohr effect is the lowering of haemoglobin's oxygen affinity by CO₂ (and H⁺), which helps unload oxygen in active tissues. The chloride shift is the exchange of HCO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ across the red-cell membrane.

questions.q: Which person is most likely to have a larger vital capacity than an average adult of the same height?
o: A person with a collapsed lung
A person whose diaphragm is weakened
questions.x: Regular endurance training strengthens the breathing muscles and increases vital capacity. Emphysema, a collapsed lung and a weak diaphragm all reduce the volume that can be breathed out after a deepest breath.

questions.q: Lungs made of millions of tiny alveoli exchange gases far better than lungs made of a few large air sacs of the same total volume. The main reason is that tiny alveoli:
o: Provide a much larger total surface area
Hold a much larger volume of air
questions.x: Dividing the same volume into many small sacs greatly increases the surface area available for diffusion. Alveoli have extremely thin walls and a dense network of capillaries.

questions.q: Which sequence shows the enzymes that act on a protein, in order, as it is digested from food into amino acids?
questions.x: Protein digestion starts with pepsin in the stomach, continues with pancreatic trypsin in the duodenum, and ends with peptidases of the small intestine, which release amino acids.

questions.q: Although little absorption takes place in the stomach, which substance can be absorbed to some extent through the stomach wall?
questions.x: The stomach can absorb some alcohol and certain drugs such as aspirin. Amino acids and fatty acids are absorbed in the small intestine, and starch must be digested before any absorption.

questions.q: Which property of plasma proteins mainly keeps them out of the glomerular filtrate?
o: Their rapid active reabsorption from Bowman's capsule
Their secretion back into the blood by the PCT
Their attachment to red blood cells
questions.x: Plasma proteins are too large to pass the filtration barrier, so they stay in the blood. Filtration works mainly by size, not by any later reabsorption or secretion.

questions.q: In severe liver failure, which substance rises to dangerous levels in the blood?
o: Urea, because the liver makes too much of it
Ammonia, because the liver can no longer convert it to urea
Uric acid, because the liver breaks down purines faster
Creatinine, because the liver makes it from muscle
questions.x: The ornithine cycle runs in the liver. If the liver fails, ammonia from deamination is not converted to urea and accumulates, poisoning the brain.

questions.q: Urine tests can show whether an athlete has taken certain banned drugs. This works because the kidneys:
o: Excrete many drugs and their breakdown products in the urine
Store drugs permanently in the bladder
Filter only drugs and no other substances
questions.x: Removing foreign substances such as drugs and their products is part of the kidney's excretory role, so traces appear in urine and can be detected.

questions.q: Kidney cells respire rapidly to power active transport. So, compared with arterial blood, blood leaving the kidney in the renal vein has:
o: More oxygen and less carbon dioxide
Less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
More plasma proteins than it received
questions.x: Tubule cells take oxygen from the peritubular blood and add carbon dioxide from respiration. Glucose is reabsorbed back, not added, and plasma proteins are not made by the kidney.

questions.q: Many people who have had one kidney stone form another later. The main reason is that:
o: Stone fragments regrow inside the bloodstream
Lithotripsy makes the kidneys produce stones
Kidney stones are passed between people by infection
The conditions that caused the first stone, such as low fluid intake, often continue
questions.x: Unless the cause, such as concentrated urine or high urinary calcium, is corrected, new crystals keep forming. Stones are not infectious and do not grow in blood.

questions.q: Amino acids in the glomerular filtrate are normally:
o: Excreted in the urine as a waste
Reabsorbed only in the collecting duct under ADH
Almost completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule
Converted into urea in the loop of Henle
questions.x: Amino acids, like glucose, are useful and are reabsorbed by active transport in the PCT, so healthy urine has almost none. ADH controls water, not amino acids.

questions.q: In the ornithine cycle, which compound is regenerated at the end so that the cycle can continue?
questions.x: When arginine is split, urea is released and ornithine is reformed, ready to combine with more ammonia and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: On a sunny winter day a person feels warm standing in sunlight although the air is cold. The heat reaches the body mainly by:
questions.x: Sunlight transfers heat as radiation, which needs no contact and does not depend on warming the air.

questions.q: Urine that has a lower solute concentration than blood plasma is described as:
questions.x: Hypotonic means less concentrated than plasma; the kidneys make it when the body has excess water and ADH is low. Hypertonic urine is more concentrated and is made when water must be saved.

questions.q: Plasmids and a donor gene are both cut with EcoRI and mixed with DNA ligase. Besides recombinant plasmids, which other product is commonly formed?
o: Plasmids that have rejoined their own ends without taking up the gene
Proteins coded by the donor gene
questions.x: The sticky ends of a cut plasmid can pair with each other, so some plasmids simply close up again without the gene. This is why bacteria must be screened afterwards to find those with the recombinant plasmid.

questions.q: Which base is found in an RNA probe but not in a DNA probe?
questions.x: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine. Adenine and guanine (and cytosine) are found in both DNA and RNA.

questions.q: The RT-PCR test used to diagnose COVID-19 first uses the enzyme reverse transcriptase because:
o: The virus's genetic material is RNA, which must be copied into DNA before PCR
The virus has a protein coat that must be digested
Human DNA must be removed before testing
Primers can bind only to protein
questions.x: PCR copies DNA, but the coronavirus genome is RNA. Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA from the viral RNA, which is then amplified and detected.

questions.q: When a high proportion of people in a community are vaccinated against measles, even unvaccinated babies are better protected. This is because:
o: The vaccine spreads from vaccinated people to the babies
Vaccinated people pass their memory cells to babies by touch
The virus cannot spread easily through a mostly immune population
The measles virus becomes harmless after a vaccination campaign
questions.x: When most people are immune, an infected person meets few susceptible contacts, so chains of transmission break. This is called herd immunity. The vaccine itself is not passed to others.

questions.q: Octane in petrol burns as 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. How many moles of CO₂ are produced per mole of octane burnt?
questions.x: The ratio CO₂ : C₈H₁₈ is 16 : 2 = 8 : 1, so each mole of octane gives 8 mol of CO₂, one for each carbon atom. 9 is the ratio for water.

questions.q: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. How many moles of nitrogen are needed to make 10 mol of ammonia?
questions.x: The ratio N₂ : NH₃ is 1 : 2, so 10 mol of NH₃ needs 10/2 = 5 mol of N₂.

questions.q: The energy of a photon of wavelength λ is given by:
questions.x: E = hν and ν = c/λ, so E = hc/λ. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

questions.q: An atom has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s². Its atomic number is:
questions.x: 18 (argon core) + 10 + 2 = 30, which is zinc.

questions.q: The number of spherical (radial) nodes in a 3s orbital is:
questions.x: An s orbital has (n − 1) spherical nodes: 1s has none, 2s one and 3s two.

questions.q: A real gas at moderate pressure has a compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT less than 1. This shows that:
o: The volume of the molecules dominates, so the gas is less compressible than an ideal gas
The gas is behaving exactly as an ideal gas
Attractive forces dominate, so the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas
The molecules have no kinetic energy
questions.x: Attractions pull molecules together, so the measured PV is smaller than nRT and Z is below 1. When molecular volume dominates, as at very high pressure, Z rises above 1.

questions.q: For real gases, which assumption of the kinetic theory remains valid?
o: Molecules are in continuous random motion
The molecules themselves have negligible volume
There are no attractive forces between molecules
The whole container volume is free for molecular motion
questions.x: Real gas molecules are still in constant random motion. The faulty postulates are those about negligible molecular volume and no attractions, which is why the free volume is less than the container volume.

questions.q: A gas is at 0 °C. To what Celsius temperature must it be heated to double its absolute temperature?
questions.x: 0 °C is 273 K; doubling gives 546 K, which is 546 − 273 = 273 °C. The 546 °C answer forgets to convert back to Celsius.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes boiling from evaporation?
o: Boiling occurs only at the surface; evaporation occurs throughout the liquid
Evaporation needs a fixed temperature; boiling occurs at any temperature
Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature for a given pressure; evaporation occurs only at the surface
Boiling cools the remaining liquid; evaporation does not
questions.x: Evaporation is a surface process at any temperature. Boiling forms vapour bubbles throughout the liquid, and only at the temperature where vapour pressure equals the external pressure.

questions.q: The anomalous behaviour of water, such as its maximum density at 4 °C, is due to:
questions.x: Hydrogen bonds arrange water molecules into an open structure in ice, which partly survives just above 0 °C; this gives water its unusual density changes.

questions.q: Many ionic crystals dissolve readily in water but not in benzene. The main reason is that:
o: Polar water molecules hydrate the ions and the energy released helps overcome the lattice energy
Water breaks the covalent bonds inside the ions
Benzene reacts with the ions to form a precipitate
Ionic crystals contain molecules that hydrogen-bond only with water
questions.x: Water's dipoles surround and stabilise the ions (hydration). Non-polar benzene cannot do this, so it cannot overcome the strong ionic attractions.

questions.q: 1 mol of CO and 1 mol of H₂O(g) are heated in a 1 dm³ closed vessel: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂. At equilibrium 0.75 mol of CO₂ is present. The value of Kc is:
questions.x: At equilibrium CO₂ = H₂ = 0.75 and CO = H₂O = 0.25 mol dm⁻³. Kc = (0.75 × 0.75)/(0.25 × 0.25) = 9.

questions.q: In soap making, common salt (NaCl) is added to make the soap (a sodium salt of a fatty acid) separate out. This works because:
o: NaCl reacts with the soap to form a new compound
The common Na⁺ ion lowers the solubility of the soap
NaCl raises the boiling point of the mixture
Cl⁻ ions break the soap down into fatty acid
questions.x: This is called salting out: the extra Na⁺ ions push the solubility equilibrium of the sodium soap back, so the soap separates.

questions.q: For an acidic buffer, the Henderson equation is:
questions.x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). More salt raises the pH; when [salt] = [acid], pH = pKa.

questions.q: Under the same conditions, which metal reacts fastest with cold water?
questions.x: The nature of the reactant affects the rate. Potassium is the most reactive of these and reacts violently; magnesium reacts with cold water only very slowly.

questions.q: Heating a sample of gas changes the shape of its Maxwell–Boltzmann plot. What happens to the total area under that plot?
o: Increases, because the molecules move faster
Stays the same, because the number of molecules is unchanged
Decreases, because the curve becomes flatter
questions.x: The total area equals the total number of molecules, which does not change. The curve only spreads out to higher energies.

questions.q: For rate = k[X][Y], the concentrations of both X and Y are tripled. The rate increases by a factor of:
questions.x: The reaction is first order in each reactant, so the factor is 3 × 3 = 9.

questions.q: In the convention ΔE = q + w, heat absorbed by the system and work done by the system are taken as:
o: Heat positive, work done by the system negative
Heat negative, work done by the system positive
questions.x: Anything that adds energy to the system is positive. Absorbed heat adds energy; work done by the system removes energy, so it is negative.

questions.q: A beaker of water boiling on a burner, with no lid, is an example of:
questions.x: Both energy (heat) and matter (steam) pass across the boundary of an open beaker, so it is an open system.

questions.q: For the reaction Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu, the reduction half-reaction is:
questions.x: Copper(II) ions gain electrons to form copper metal. Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ is the oxidation half-reaction.

questions.q: In the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, the substance that is oxidised is:
questions.x: Hydrogen goes from 0 in H₂ to +1 in H₂O, so it is oxidised; copper falls from +2 to 0 and is reduced.

questions.q: How many sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds are present in hydrogen cyanide, H–C≡N?
questions.x: The C–H single bond is one σ bond. The C≡N triple bond has one σ and two π bonds. Total: 2 σ and 2 π.

questions.q: The C–H bond energy quoted in tables (about 414 kJ mol⁻¹) is called an average bond energy because:
o: All C–H bonds in every compound have exactly this energy
It is measured only for liquid compounds
It includes the energy needed to melt the compound
The energy needed to break each successive C–H bond in CH₄ is slightly different
questions.x: Removing the first, second, third and fourth H from CH₄ needs different amounts of energy. The table value is the mean, and it also varies a little from compound to compound.

questions.q: A bond has 20% ionic character. If it were 100% ionic, its dipole moment would be 5.5 D. Its observed dipole moment is:
questions.x: Observed μ = 20% of 5.5 D = 0.20 × 5.5 = 1.1 D. 4.4 D is the 80% remainder, and 27.5 D comes from dividing by 0.20.

questions.q: When Group II metals react with water they form hydroxides, M(OH)₂. Down the group, the solubility of these hydroxides in water:
o: Decreases, so Ba(OH)₂ is the least soluble
Increases, so Mg(OH)₂ is the most soluble
Increases, so Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble
questions.x: Mg(OH)₂ is almost insoluble, Ca(OH)₂ is slightly soluble and Ba(OH)₂ is fairly soluble, so solutions become more strongly alkaline down the group.

questions.q: Down a group, electronegativity decreases mainly because:
o: Nuclear charge decreases down the group
The number of valence electrons decreases
Atomic size increases, so the nucleus attracts bonding electrons less strongly
questions.x: New shells are added, the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so attraction for it falls despite the larger nuclear charge.

questions.q: d-block elements are called transition elements mainly because they:
o: All have completely filled d subshells in their atoms
Lie between the s-block and p-block, with properties intermediate between them
Change into other elements by radioactive decay
Have their last electron entering an s orbital
questions.x: They sit between the reactive s-block metals and the p-block elements, and their properties show a transition between the two. Their last electron enters a d orbital, and most have partly filled d subshells.

questions.q: Which statement about 2-methylbut-2-ene, CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂, is correct?
o: It has cis and trans isomers, because it contains a C=C bond
It has no cis–trans isomers, because one doubly bonded carbon carries two identical CH₃ groups
It is optically active, because it contains a chiral carbon
It has cis and trans isomers, because it has three methyl groups
questions.x: Geometric isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of the C=C. Here one carbon carries two CH₃ groups, so swapping them gives the same molecule.

questions.q: Converting 1,2-dibromoethane into ethyne needs two eliminations. What happens to the hybridisation of the carbons?
questions.x: The dibromide has only single bonds (sp³). The first elimination gives bromoethene with a double bond (sp²); the second gives the triple bond of ethyne (sp).

questions.q: Counting single and double bonds in CH₂=CH₂, ethene contains:
questions.x: There are four C–H σ bonds and one C–C σ bond, making 5 σ, plus one π bond in the double bond.

questions.q: Free-radical chlorination of methane usually gives a mixture of products because:
o: Methane contains carbon atoms of different types
Chlorine radicals add to methane at several positions
The chloromethane formed can itself react with chlorine radicals
Some methane always changes into ethene first
questions.x: CH₃Cl still has C–H bonds, so Cl• can attack it to give CH₂Cl₂, then CHCl₃ and CCl₄. All four hydrogens in methane are equivalent, and no addition takes place.

questions.q: Ethyne is hydrated by passing it into dilute sulphuric acid. The catalyst used is:
questions.x: Hydration of ethyne needs dilute H₂SO₄ with HgSO₄ (mercuric sulphate) as catalyst. Nickel is used for hydrogenation.

questions.q: Hex-1-ene, hexane and benzene are each shaken with cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄. The purple colour disappears with:
questions.x: Only an alkene with a localised C=C bond is oxidised by Baeyer's reagent to a diol. Benzene and hexane leave the purple colour unchanged.

questions.q: An alkene C₄H₈ gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃) and methanal on ozonolysis followed by Zn/H₂O. The alkene is:
questions.x: Joining the two carbonyl carbons with a C=C gives (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene. But-1-ene would give propanal and methanal, and but-2-ene only ethanal.

questions.q: Ethylbenzene is treated with chlorine in the presence of FeCl₃ in the dark. The main products are:
questions.x: An alkyl group is ortho/para-directing, and the Lewis acid catalyst gives ring substitution. Side-chain chlorination would need sunlight instead.

questions.q: An alkyl halide undergoes elimination by the E1 mechanism. If the base concentration is doubled while [RX] stays the same, the rate:
questions.x: In E1 the slow step is ionisation of RX alone, so rate = k[RX] and the base does not appear in the rate equation. Doubling would be true for E2.

questions.q: Using IUPAC rules, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Br should be named:
questions.x: The longest chain has four carbons. Numbering from the CH₂Br end gives locants 1 and 3, lower than 2 and 4 from the other end. The chain is butane, not pentane, because one CH₃ is a branch.

questions.q: The mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol from nitration of phenol can be separated by steam distillation, because 2-nitrophenol:
o: Has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, so it is more volatile
Has intermolecular hydrogen bonding, so it is less volatile
Has a much larger molar mass
questions.x: In 2-nitrophenol the –OH and –NO₂ are close enough to hydrogen-bond within the molecule, so it does not associate with its neighbours and distils with steam. 4-Nitrophenol hydrogen-bonds between molecules and stays behind. The two have equal molar masses.

questions.q: Which reagent can be used to distinguish phenol from cyclohexanol?
questions.x: Phenol decolourises bromine water at once and gives a white precipitate because its ring is activated; cyclohexanol, a saturated alcohol, gives neither. Both give hydrogen with sodium.

questions.q: Which reagent gives a brick-red precipitate with ethanal but no change with propanone?
questions.x: Ethanal reduces the Cu²⁺ of Fehling's solution to red Cu₂O; propanone is not oxidised. Both compounds react with 2,4-DNPH, with sodium hydrogensulphite and with iodine in alkali, so those cannot tell them apart.

questions.q: 2-Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, is treated with ozone and the ozonide is then warmed with zinc dust and water. The products are:
questions.x: The C=C bond is cut and each carbon becomes C=O: (CH₃)₂C= gives (CH₃)₂C=O (propanone) and =CH₂ gives HCHO (methanal).

questions.q: Which type of alcohol can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms?
questions.x: Primary alcohols are oxidised first to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols give ketones, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation.

questions.q: Invertase hydrolyses sucrose: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose). Complete hydrolysis of 342 g of sucrose gives what mass of glucose? (C 12, H 1, O 16)
questions.x: Sucrose = 342 g mol⁻¹, so 342 g is 1 mol, giving 1 mol of glucose = 180 g. 360 g counts glucose and fructose together.

questions.q: Insulin, a protein hormone made in the pancreas, controls the:
o: Level of glucose in the blood
questions.x: Insulin lowers blood glucose by helping cells take it up. Oxygen transport is the job of haemoglobin, and muscle contraction that of actin and myosin.

questions.q: The synthetic fibre Orlon (acrylic) is obtained by polymerising which monomer?
questions.x: Acrylic fibres are addition polymers of acrylonitrile, CH₂=CHCN. Chloroethene gives PVC, and ethane-1,2-diol is a monomer of polyesters.

questions.q: A vector has an x-component of −8 units and a y-component of +6 units. Its magnitude and the quadrant in which it lies are:
questions.x: Magnitude = √(64 + 36) = 10 units. A negative x-component with a positive y-component places the vector in the second quadrant.

questions.q: A 2 kg mass hangs from a string and is pulled upward with an acceleration of 5 m s⁻². Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the tension in the string is:
questions.x: T − mg = ma, so T = m(g + a) = 2 × 15 = 30 N. 10 N wrongly subtracts the acceleration from g.

questions.q: A projectile is launched with speed v at angle θ above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal and vertical velocity components at time t are:
o: v cos θ − gt and v sin θ
v cos θ and v sin θ − gt
v sin θ and v cos θ − gt
v cos θ and v sin θ − ½gt²
questions.x: The horizontal component stays v cos θ. The vertical component starts at v sin θ and decreases by g each second: v sin θ − gt. ½gt² belongs to displacement, not velocity.

questions.q: Newton's second law written as F = ma is a special case of F = Δp/Δt. It holds only when:
o: The velocity of the body stays constant
The mass of the body stays constant
The force acts for a very short time
questions.x: F = Δ(mv)/Δt = m(Δv/Δt) = ma only if m does not change. For changing mass, such as a rocket, the momentum form must be used.

questions.q: A swimmer pushes the water backward with her hands and moves forward. This is an example of:
questions.x: The swimmer's push on the water (action) is matched by an equal and opposite push of the water on the swimmer (reaction), which drives her forward.

questions.q: A 5 kg body at rest on a smooth surface is acted on by a constant force of 10 N for 3 s. The distance it covers in this time is:
questions.x: a = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m s⁻², and s = ½at² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 m. 18 m forgets the ½.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, at what height above the point of projection are its kinetic and potential energies equal? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.x: Total energy = ½ × 0.5 × 20² = 100 J. When KE = PE, PE = 50 J, so h = 50 ÷ (0.5 × 10) = 10 m, half the maximum height of 20 m.

questions.q: When a torch is switched on, the main energy changes taking place are:
o: Chemical energy of the cells → electrical energy → light and heat
questions.x: The cells convert stored chemical energy into electrical energy, which the bulb converts into light and some heat.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car climbs a straight road at a constant 10 m s⁻¹. The road rises 1 m for every 20 m along it (sin θ = 1/20). Ignoring friction, the power needed is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: Force needed = mg sin θ = 12 000 × 1/20 = 600 N. P = Fv = 600 × 10 = 6000 W = 6 kW. Using mg v without sin θ gives 120 kW.

questions.q: How many radians are there in 45°?
questions.x: Multiply degrees by π/180: 45 × π/180 = π/4 rad.

questions.q: For a point at distance r from the axis of a body with angular acceleration α, the tangential acceleration is:
questions.x: Linear and angular quantities are linked by the radius: s = rθ, v = rω and a = rα.

questions.q: A volume V of liquid enters a pipe where the pressure is P₁ and later leaves where the pressure is P₂. Which expression gives the total work that the surrounding liquid does on it?
questions.x: Work in at the inlet is P₁V and work at the outlet is −P₂V, so the net work is (P₁ − P₂)V. This is then equated to the gain in kinetic energy.

questions.q: Compared with laminar flow at the same rate, pushing a liquid through a pipe in turbulent flow requires:
o: A larger pressure difference between the ends of the pipe
A smaller pressure difference between the ends of the pipe
The same pressure difference, since flow type has no effect
questions.x: Eddies in turbulent flow dissipate extra energy as heat, so a larger pressure difference must do more work to keep the same flow going.

questions.q: The radius of a pipe carrying an ideal fluid is tripled at a wide section. The speed of the fluid there becomes:
o: One ninth of its original value
One third of its original value
questions.x: Area ∝ r², so tripling r makes A nine times larger. With Av constant, v falls to one ninth.

questions.q: The tension in a stretched rope is increased while the hand shaking it keeps the same frequency. The waves on the rope will now have:
o: A greater speed and a shorter wavelength
The same speed and a longer wavelength
A greater speed and a longer wavelength
A smaller speed and a shorter wavelength
questions.x: Wave speed on a rope is v = √(T/μ), so a larger tension gives a larger speed. With f fixed, λ = v/f also increases.

questions.q: Water waves of wavelength 2 m travel at 4 m s⁻¹ in deep water. They move into shallow water, where their speed falls to 2 m s⁻¹. Their wavelength in the shallow water is:
questions.x: The frequency does not change: f = 4/2 = 2 Hz. In shallow water λ = v/f = 2/2 = 1 m.

questions.q: The velocity of a progressive wave means:
o: The maximum speed of a vibrating particle of the medium
The speed at which particles of the medium travel away from the source
The number of waves produced per second
The speed with which the disturbance, such as a crest, moves forward through the medium
questions.x: Wave velocity is the distance moved by the wave form per unit time (v = fλ). It is different from particle velocity, which changes continuously as each particle vibrates.

questions.q: A fork of unknown frequency gives 4 beats per second with a 256 Hz fork. When the prongs of the unknown fork are filed slightly, which raises its frequency, the beats drop to 2 per second. The original frequency of the unknown fork was:
questions.x: It was either 252 Hz or 260 Hz. Raising 260 Hz would increase the beats, so it must have been 252 Hz, rising towards 256 Hz to give fewer beats.

questions.q: The amplitude of a simple pendulum's swing is reduced from 4° to 2°. Its time period:
questions.x: For small swings T = 2π√(l/g), which does not depend on the amplitude. Only the length and g decide the period.

questions.q: A small source sends sound out equally in all directions in open air, with no energy lost. At 2 m from the source the intensity is I. At 4 m from the source the intensity is:
questions.x: The same power spreads over a sphere of area 4πr². Doubling r makes the area four times as large, so the intensity becomes I/4.

questions.q: A heat engine can never give out more work in a cycle than the heat it takes in during that cycle. This follows from:
o: The law of conservation of energy
questions.x: The first law is energy conservation: over a cycle ΔU = 0, so the work output cannot exceed the net heat input.

questions.q: When comparing the heat needed by different gases, molar specific heat is often more useful than specific heat because:
o: One mole of every gas contains the same number of molecules
One kilogram of every gas has the same volume
Specific heat cannot be measured for a gas
Molar specific heat does not depend on the gas at all
questions.x: One mole of any substance has the same number of molecules (Avogadro's number), so molar specific heat compares heat needed per molecule on a fair basis.

questions.q: On a sunny day the sand on a beach becomes much hotter than the sea water. The main reason is that:
o: Sand has a much higher specific heat than water
Sand receives far more sunlight than the sea
Sand has a much lower specific heat than water
Water cannot absorb heat from the Sun
questions.x: For the same heat per kilogram, a substance with lower specific heat has a bigger temperature rise. Water's high specific heat keeps it cooler.

questions.q: Two equal positive point charges are fixed a distance apart. Moving outward along their perpendicular bisector, starting from the midpoint, the magnitude of the electric field:
o: Is greatest at the midpoint and falls steadily
Is zero at the midpoint, rises to a maximum and then falls off far away
Is the same at every point on the bisector
Is zero at every point on the bisector
questions.x: At the midpoint the fields cancel (neutral point). Moving out, the components along the bisector add, so the field grows; far away it weakens again with distance. So it rises to a maximum and then falls.

questions.q: In the field-line pattern of two equal positive point charges, the field line that leaves one charge directly along the line towards the other charge:
o: Goes straight on and ends on the other charge
Forms a closed loop back to the first charge
Stops at the neutral point midway; no line passes from one charge to the other
Bends at right angles and continues along the bisector without stopping
questions.x: Field lines end only on negative charges. Between two like charges the fields cancel at the neutral point, so the joining line runs into the neutral point from each side; no line links the charges.

questions.q: Moving along the direction of an electric field line, the electric potential:
questions.x: Field lines point from high potential to low potential, so potential falls along the direction of the field.

questions.q: Electric current through a conductor is defined as the:
o: Rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t
Product of charge and time, I = Qt
Charge per unit volume of the conductor
questions.x: Current is the charge passing a cross-section per unit time, I = Q/t. Energy per unit charge is potential difference or emf, not current.

questions.q: For a metal wire, a graph of resistance against temperature in °C over the normal range is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line rising with temperature that does not pass through the origin
questions.x: R = R₀(1 + αt): R rises linearly with t and equals R₀ (not zero) at 0 °C, so the line has an intercept and does not pass through the origin.

questions.q: A charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform field feels a force of 4 × 10⁻¹² N. At the same speed, moving at 30° to the field, it feels (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87):
questions.x: F = qvB sin θ, so the force falls to 4 × 10⁻¹² × sin 30° = 2 × 10⁻¹² N. Using cos 30° gives 3.5 × 10⁻¹², which is wrong.

questions.q: A bar magnet is dropped through a complete, uncut copper ring held horizontally. As it approaches the ring, its acceleration is:
questions.x: The changing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law), so there is an upward force and the acceleration is less than g.

questions.q: On a 50 Hz mains supply, the current in a circuit reaches its peak 2.5 ms after the voltage does. The phase lag of the current is:
questions.x: T = 1/50 = 20 ms. A delay of 2.5 ms is 2.5/20 = 1/8 of a cycle, and 1/8 × 360° = 45°.

questions.q: Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelength?
questions.x: Radio waves lie at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the electromagnetic spectrum; gamma rays are at the other end.

questions.q: Electrons are only just released from a surface whose work function is 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the longest wavelength of light able to do this? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.x: Threshold wavelength λ₀ = hc/φ = (1.98 × 10⁻²⁵)/(6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3 × 10⁻⁷ m = 300 nm. Longer wavelengths carry too little energy per photon.

questions.q: An atom emits a spectral line of wavelength 600 nm. What is the energy difference between the two levels involved? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.x: ΔE = hc/λ = (1.98 × 10⁻²⁵)/(6 × 10⁻⁷) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Leaving λ in nm gives the 10⁻²⁸ value.

questions.q: A Geiger counter near a long-lived source records counts in many equal 10-second intervals. The counts vary irregularly from one interval to the next. This shows that decay is:
questions.x: Because each nucleus decays at an unpredictable moment, the number of decays in equal intervals fluctuates even though the average rate stays steady.

questions.q: The mass number A of a nucleus is the number of:
questions.x: The mass number counts all the nucleons, that is protons plus neutrons. The number of protons alone is the atomic number Z.

questions.q: Bilal's mother came back into the kitchen and stopped. The fish she had left on the table to cool was gone. A trail of small bones led from the table to the sofa, where the family cat lay on a cushion, slowly licking its whiskers. What can be inferred from the passage?
o: The cat had eaten the fish
Someone had put the fish in the fridge
A visitor had taken the fish away
questions.x: The trail of bones leads to the cat, which is licking its whiskers, so the clues point to the cat. Nothing in the passage mentions Bilal, the fridge or a visitor.

questions.q: Sara said, "I am hungry." In reported speech this becomes:
o: Sara said that I was hungry.
Sara said that she is being hungry.
Sara said that she had been hungry now.
Sara said that she was hungry.
questions.x: After a past reporting verb, 'am' changes to 'was' and 'I' changes to 'she'.

questions.q: In "The children played cricket behind the school", the phrase 'behind the school' is:
o: A noun phrase acting as object
questions.x: It tells where the children played, so it modifies the verb as an adverb phrase of place; it has no verb, so it is not a clause.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Ali is very good at ___ maths problems."
questions.x: A preposition such as 'at' is followed by a gerund (-ing form).

questions.q: Find the error: "One of the girls has left his bag at home."
questions.x: The antecedent 'One of the girls' refers to a girl, so the pronoun should be 'her'; 'has left' correctly agrees with the singular 'One'.

questions.q: Which group of words is a phrase, NOT a clause?
questions.x: A clause has its own subject and verb; 'after the long exam' has no verb, so it is a phrase.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Don't forget ___ off the lights before you leave the lab."
questions.x: 'Forget + to-infinitive' is used for something one must remember to do; 'forget + gerund' refers to a past action.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "My elder brother ____ in a bank in Karachi."
questions.x: 'My elder brother' is a singular third-person subject, so the present-simple verb takes -s: 'works'.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "The number of applicants for the course ____ risen sharply this year."
questions.x: 'The number of ...' refers to one number, so it is singular: 'has risen'. It is 'a number of' (meaning many) that takes a plural verb.

questions.q: Four books P, Q, R and S stand in a row. S is to the left of P, P is to the left of Q, and R is to the right of Q. Which statement must be true?
o: P is at the right end
R is second from the left
Q is third from the left
questions.x: The only order that fits is S, P, Q, R from the left, so Q is third. P is second, R is at the right end and S is not next to Q.

questions.q: Find the next pair: BD, FH, JL, NP, ?
questions.x: Each letter of the pair moves 4 places forward: N to R and P to T, giving RT.

questions.q: Find the next group: AZB, CYD, EXF, ?
questions.x: The first and third letters run A B, C D, E F, then G H; the middle letters run Z, Y, X, then W. So the group is GWH.

questions.q: Sana is the sister of Imran. Imran is the son of Rehana. Rehana's father is Akbar. How is Sana related to Akbar?
questions.x: Sana is Imran's sister, so she is also Rehana's daughter. Rehana is Akbar's daughter, so Sana is Akbar's granddaughter.

questions.q: Five houses in a row, numbered 1 to 5 from the left, are painted blue, green, red, white and yellow, one colour each. The red house is in the middle. The blue house is at the left end. The green house is immediately to the left of the white house. What colour is house 2?
questions.x: Blue is 1 and red is 3. Green and white need two side-by-side places, which can only be 4 and 5, so house 2 is yellow.

questions.q: Statement: A pharmacy finds that many bottles in a new batch of cough syrup have broken seals. Courses of action: I. The pharmacy should stop selling all its medicines. II. The pharmacy should not sell the bottles with broken seals and should report the batch to the supplier. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The problem is limited to one batch, so holding back those bottles and reporting them is the right decision. Stopping all sales is far too extreme.

questions.q: Statement: Many children in a neighbourhood have not been vaccinated against measles. Courses of action: I. Health workers should run a vaccination drive in the area. II. Parents should be told why the vaccine is important. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: A vaccination drive reaches the children directly, and informing parents helps them accept it. Both actions address the problem.

questions.q: Statement I: Students cleared the garbage from their street. Statement II: Fewer flies and mosquitoes were seen in the street afterwards. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: Garbage provides breeding places and food for flies and mosquitoes. Removing it led to fewer insects.

questions.q: Statement I: Onion prices in the markets rose sharply. Statement II: Floods destroyed a large part of the onion crop. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: Losing much of the crop cuts the supply of onions, which pushes prices up. The flood damage is the cause, even though it is written second.
